title: AgentDevel: Reframing Self-Evolving LLM Agents as Release Engineering
mutable_substrate: A complete executable agent blueprint: prompts, orchestration code, and tool-invocation internals.
optimization_operator: An LLM uses an executed diagnostic program and its report to synthesize exactly one scoped release candidate and declared change intent per iteration.
feedback_selection: Optional deterministic scorers plus an implementation-blind critic produce per-example pass and symptom records; a configurable gate compares fail-to-pass fixes, pass-to-fail regressions, and intent alignment before atomic promotion.
archive_memory: One canonical release line with version-controlled diagnostic scripts, RC diffs, critic outputs, and flip lists; the previous diagnostic script is a soft reference, but rejected candidate blueprints are not maintained as a population archive.
validation_strategy: All diagnosis, RC evaluation, gating, and stopping use a fixed TrainSet; the held-out TestSet is evaluated once after development. No repeated-run uncertainty or adaptive-holdout control is reported.
adaptation_mode: Offline, iterative release engineering with one candidate at a time; not runtime adaptation.
principal_results: SWE-bench Lite improves from 11.00% to 22.00% (+11.00 points); the cited SWE-agent result is 18.00% and was not rerun under the same setup.
SWE-bench Verified improves from 15.00% to 30.00% (+15.00 points); the cited GPT-4o scaffolded result is 33.20% and was not rerun under the same setup.
WebArena improves from 17.00% to 35.50% in the main table (+18.50 points), while the full-system ablation separately reports 34.2% without reconciling the difference.
StableToolBench improves from 54.00% to 73.50% SoWR (+19.50 points), above the cited 70.20% DFS value.
On WebArena, removing the flip gate raises the ablation test metric from 34.2 to 35.0 but increases P2F transitions from 18 to 95, the P2F rate from 3.1% to 14.8%, and bad releases from 0 to 4.

On WebArena, removing executable diagnosis lowers the test metric from 34.2 to 31.8 and F2P count from 214 to 150; exposing the blueprint to the critic raises train pass from 78.5 to 83.5 but lowers test performance to 32.5 and raises P2F rate to 6.7%.

In the 11-iteration StableToolBench case, an RC with 42 fixes is rejected because it also causes 28 regressions; accepted rows sum to 142 F2P and 25 P2F transitions, while three rejected rows sum to 53 F2P and 46 P2F.
limitations: Gate thresholds, stopping rules, hit rate, FTP/P2P, bad-release threshold, split sizes, candidate budgets, seeds, and exact blueprints are not fully specified.
Repeated adaptive reuse of one TrainSet can overfit even though the TestSet is held out until final evaluation.
The 35.50 WebArena main result and 34.2 full ablation result are not reconciled.
Prior-work numbers are cited rather than rerun under matched models, tools, splits, and budgets.
No confidence intervals, multi-seed replication, critic-reliability study, token/API cost, or wall-clock cost is reported.
One RC and one canonical line improve auditability but reduce exploration and retain no archive of useful rejected variants.
Only single-agent, single-repository or environment settings are evaluated; multi-agent and nonstationary deployment remain open.
The open symptom taxonomy has no label merge, deprecation, or drift-control mechanism.
safety_controls: Implementation-blind critic separation to reduce evaluator–implementation entanglement.
Programmatic scorers override critic pass judgments when available.
Paired F2P/P2F regression accounting on the same TrainSet.
Atomic accept-or-discard promotion on a canonical version line with saved diffs and flip lists.
Held-out TestSet excluded from development decisions.

No explicit sandbox, permission model, dependency policy, secret isolation, or human approval is reported for generated diagnostic scripts and agent code changes; non-regression is reduced empirically, not formally guaranteed.

explicit_predecessors.name: Continuous integration and software release engineering
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The paper reframes agent evolution around release candidates, regression checks, atomic promotion, versioned artifacts, and stopping criteria drawn from software release practice.

explicit_predecessors.name: Darwin Gödel Machine
explicit_predecessors.evidence: Related work names archive/population-oriented self-improvement and contrasts it with AgentDevel's single canonical release line and gated RC promotion.

explicit_predecessors.name: Live-SWE-Agent
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The paper cites self-modifying coding agents while positioning AgentDevel as offline release engineering with paired regression evidence.

explicit_predecessors.name: Reflexion and Self-Refine
explicit_predecessors.evidence: AgentDevel contrasts cognition-centered textual reflection and revision with artifact-centered executable diagnosis, versioning, and promotion gates.

explicit_predecessors.name: PromptBreeder and Tree of Thoughts
explicit_predecessors.evidence: These are cited as candidate-search approaches; AgentDevel instead proposes one auditable RC from the canonical blueprint per iteration.

explicit_predecessors.name: MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, G-Eval, and AlpacaEval
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The paper builds on LLM-as-judge evaluation but restricts the critic to implementation-blind observable symptoms and defers to hard scorers when present.

explicit_predecessors.name: SWE-agent
explicit_predecessors.evidence: The main table compares AgentDevel's 22.00% SWE-bench Lite resolved rate to a cited 18.00% SWE-agent result, without a matched rerun.

open_questions: Can a flip gate provide statistically defensible, severity-weighted non-regression guarantees rather than heuristic risk reduction?
How should adaptive TrainSet reuse be controlled across many release candidates?
Can bounded branches or archives recover exploration while retaining a canonical release line?
How robust is implementation blindness when traces leak implementation behavior?
What sandboxing and human-review controls are necessary for LLM-generated diagnostic code and blueprint diffs?
What are the token, execution, monetary, and wall-clock costs per accepted improvement?
Do these controls reduce production incidents under distribution shift, not just benchmark regressions?
How should open symptom taxonomies be merged, deprecated, and monitored for drift?
Would independent critic, diagnosis, synthesis, and gate models reduce correlated errors?
Why do the main and ablation tables report different WebArena full-system scores, and how exactly are hit rate, FTP/P2P, and bad-release thresholds defined?
